pages.task: A drive runs a 400 V, 50 Hz motor at 25 Hz. What voltage does it give the motor?
pages.why: About 200 V. Below rated speed, a simple drive holds the volts per hertz about steady. That is 400 ÷ 50 = 8 V per hertz, and 8 × 25 = 200 V. Yet its DC link sits at a steady 540 V. So the switching must set both the voltage and the frequency.

pages.text: With D following a sine between 20% and 80%, the pulses are wide where the dashed average is high. The average traces a sine from 108 V to 432 V.

options: 540 V, as the top switch joins the link
pages.task: At the cursor, the top switch is on for 80% of each switching cycle. What is the leg's average voltage there?
pages.why: 432 V. D × 540 V = 0.8 × 540 = 432 V. That is the top of this leg's sine.

pages.text: Each edge sits where the sine crosses the triangle. Near the sine's peak, the reference is above it for 80% of each cycle.

pages.name: At the zero
pages.task: At the cursor the reference crosses zero, halfway up the triangle. For what share of each switching cycle is the top switch on?
pages.why: 50%. The reference sits halfway up the triangle. So it is above the triangle for half of each cycle. The average is 0.5 × 540 = 270 V. That is the middle of this leg's sine.

pages.name: The H-bridge
pages.text: The winding sees pulses of ±540 V. Their average is a sine peaking at 324 V each way, 229 V rms.

pages.name: The winding's average
pages.task: The first leg's top switch is on 75% of the time. So the mirror leg's is on 25%. What average voltage does the winding see?
pages.why: 270 V. The first leg averages 0.75 × 540 = 405 V. The mirror leg averages 0.25 × 540 = 135 V. The winding sits between them, so it sees 405 − 135 = 270 V.

pages.name: The winding smooths it
pages.text: At 3 kHz the sawtooth is about a third as tall as at 1 kHz. The sine and its 382 V rms are unchanged.

pages.name: Twice the carrier
pages.task: You double the carrier frequency to 2 kHz. What happens to the frequency of the motor's current?
pages.why: It stays at 50 Hz, the reference's frequency. The faster carrier only makes the sawtooth finer. But every switching edge makes heat in the switch, as lesson 4 showed. So a faster carrier buys a smoother current with hotter switches.

pages.name: 200 V at 25 Hz
options: The carrier, to half its frequency
The DC link, down to 200 V
pages.task: The drive must give the motor 200 V at 25 Hz, from the same 540 V link. What does it change?
pages.why: Reference to 25 Hz, depth to 60%. The frequency follows the reference. The voltage follows the depth: 200 ÷ 331 = 0.60. At 60% the readout gives 198 V, near enough 200 V. Sine-triangle PWM tops out at 331 V from this link.

pages.name: Dead time
pages.text: With no dead time, both switches in a leg conduct at every edge. A red path crosses the link. At 20 µs the red is gone. The dashed average drops about 22 V against the current. The current has a small flat near each zero.

pages.name: A longer gap
options: Nothing, as a longer gap is only safer
pages.task: The dead time is raised to 100 µs. What happens to the motor's current?
pages.why: It flattens near each zero. Each gap costs voltage against the current. Now it costs five times as much. Near each zero the current is small. So the loss stalls it. Dead time trades two faults. Too short shorts the link. Too long distorts the output. So it is kept as short as the turn-off allows.

pages.task: An online UPS keeps its battery on the DC link. The mains supply fails. What does the load see?
pages.why: No break. In double conversion the inverter feeds the load all the time. It runs from the DC link. When the mains fails, the battery holds up the link. The inverter carries on. That is zero transfer time. A drive is the same chain, without the battery, feeding a motor. A shore converter is the same chain again, turning 50 Hz into 60 Hz.
